paper.title: Large Language Models as Tool Makers
paper.central_claim: LATM: a powerful LLM acts once as tool maker (writes and verifies a Python utility function and call demonstrations) and a lightweight LLM acts as tool user; with a dispatcher forming a functional cache this lets a cheaper model match a strong model on reasoning tasks at lower serving cost.

provenance.notes: actual_model/session_id/receipt_ref not exposed to the worker in this subagent context; model_type is the configured type only.

sections_read: Appendix A (dispatcher), B (limitations), C (prompts), D (wrapped tools), E (dataset construction)

evidence.quote: However, the applicability of these tool-using methods is largely contingent on the availability of suitable tools.
evidence.support_explanation: Author gap: tool use depends on human-supplied tools.

evidence.quote: With GPT-4 as the tool maker and GPT-3.5 as the tool user, LATM demonstrates performance equivalent to using GPT-4 for both roles, but with a significantly reduced inference cost.
evidence.support_explanation: Central claim (performance equivalence at lower cost); cost reduction is argued by formula, not measured.

evidence.quote: Tool Verification: In this stage, the tool maker generates unit tests using validation samples and subsequently executes these tests on the proposed tool.
evidence.support_explanation: Admission test: unit tests built by the tool maker from 3 validation samples with known answers and executed; the unit tests also provide the wrapped demonstrations.

evidence.quote: Tool Wrapping: If the execution or verification fails over a preset threshold, the Tool Making stage is viewed as failed.
evidence.support_explanation: Failure rule: tool-making fails after the retry threshold; a failed tool is not admitted.

evidence.quote: We set the maximal retry times to be 3 for the tool-proposing and tool-verification stages.
we only observe 2 cases out of the 60 trials that the tool maker can correct its mistakes with the guide of error messages.
evidence.support_explanation: Verification-driven repair almost never happens (2/60), so the verification stage mainly supplies call demonstrations; no ablation of verification.

evidence.quote: We divide each dataset into training, validation, and test sets, containing 3, 3, and 240 instances, respectively.
evidence.support_explanation: Tool built from 3+3 instances, evaluated on 240 test instances per task; six hand-picked algorithmic task types.

evidence.quote: The results demonstrate that with the help of the tool
evidence.support_explanation: Table 2: GPT-3.5 CoT vs LATM accuracy: Logical Deduction 66.4->79.7, Tracking Shuffled 61.6->99.6, Dyck 20.4->92.2, Word Sorting 59.2->98.3, Chinese Remainder 0.0->100.0, Schedule Meeting 18.9->100.0; GPT-4 CoT vs LATM: 88.8/86.6, 100/100, 63.6/87.5, 90.9/99.1, 0/100, 55.6/100 (single run, no intervals).

evidence.quote: Success is measured by the correct identification of the tool.
evidence.support_explanation: Dispatcher evaluated only for routing accuracy on 100 mixed samples (95%+-2% over five constructions; 96%+-3% for requesting tool-making), not end-to-end cost or accuracy.

evidence.quote: These new instances are then cached until a sufficient number are amassed to craft a new tool, further enriching the functional cache
evidence.support_explanation: Cache growth rule described, threshold unspecified; no end-to-end stream experiment with tool creation.

evidence.quote: either solving it with a powerful model or, if necessary, invoking a human labeler.
evidence.support_explanation: New-task handling can fall back to a human labeler.

evidence.quote: For hard tasks like Logical Deduction and Tracking Shuffled Objects, GPT-3.5 Turbo fails in all trials, showing the necessity of using a more powerful model as tool maker
evidence.support_explanation: Tool-maker ablation: 5 trials per model per task; GPT-4 success 3/5,4/5,5/5,5/5,5/5,3/5 vs GPT-3.5 0/5,0/5,5/5,5/5,5/5,0/5.

evidence.quote: And the major failure reason is that the tool is not general enough and may only work on the training samples.
evidence.support_explanation: Failure mode: overfit tools that pass only the demonstration instances.

evidence.quote: We observe that using CoT from a large model has a similar or even worse performance than human-written CoT
evidence.support_explanation: Control: reusing GPT-4 chain-of-thought as the "tool" does not help (Logical Deduction 36.8, Tracking 63.2) vs LATM 79.7/99.6.

evidence.quote: In this study, we have not addressed these control and safety issues in depth, and our work has some limitations.
An exciting avenue for future research is enabling the tool maker to refine and upgrade existing tools
evidence.support_explanation: No update, versioning or retirement of existing tools in the method.

evidence.quote: This novel approach, combined with the strategic division of labor between the tool maker and tool user, has the potential to considerably reduce the average cost of serving a sequence of requests while maintaining high performance.
evidence.support_explanation: Cost claim stated as potential; Table 2 gives asymptotic costs O(nc+C) vs O(nC) with C over 15x c, no measured dollars.

evidence.quote: We also constructed the Scheduling Meeting task to demonstrate the effectiveness of LATM in real-world scenarios.
evidence.support_explanation: One task is author-constructed from a template; the algorithmic solution is trivial and the test distribution matches the demonstration template.

evidence.quote: The tool user can be either the same or a different LLM from the tool maker.
evidence.support_explanation: Tool user is varied (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, older GPT-3 models) with one fixed GPT-4-made tool.

signatures.object: Python utility function + wrapped call demonstrations (a "tool"), one per task type; baseline = no tool (CoT)
signatures.information: 3 training demonstrations and 3 validation instances with answers; execution errors; no test instances
signatures.operation: GPT-4 proposes a generic function from demonstrations (retry <=3), writes unit tests converting each validation question into a call, executes, wraps function + test-derived demonstrations
signatures.conditions: task has a programmatic solution; strong tool maker (GPT-3.5 fails on hard tasks)
signatures.feedback: execution errors and assertion results on 3 validation instances
signatures.selection_rule: pass all unit tests within retry threshold, else tool-making fails
signatures.persistence: wrapped tool stored per task type (functional cache)
signatures.later_use: tool-user LLM receives the wrapped tool as a prompt and writes a function call per instance
signatures.claimed_effect: GPT-3.5 with tool matches GPT-4 CoT on six tasks at lower cost
signatures.failure_boundary: non-general tools that overfit the 3 samples; tool-making fails for hard tasks with weaker makers; algorithmic tasks only

signatures.information: incoming request and tool API descriptions
signatures.operation: lightweight LLM chooses an existing tool or flags unseen task to trigger tool making (after enough cached instances)
signatures.conditions: threshold for enough instances unspecified; human labeler fallback
signatures.feedback: none beyond routing correctness measured offline
signatures.later_use: routing future instances to cached tools
signatures.failure_boundary: no end-to-end stream run; no tool update

gap.author_gap: Tool-using LLMs need suitable tools to exist; creating tools is left to humans; serving every request with a strong LLM is costly.
gap.checked_gap: Cost half is plausible by arithmetic (GPT-4 over 15x GPT-3.5) but unmeasured; tool-availability half is directly addressed. No evidence that existing agents were blocked in practice.

claims.text: A tool made by GPT-4 lets GPT-3.5 Turbo reach GPT-4-CoT-level accuracy on six task types, far above GPT-3.5 CoT
claims.setting: Logical Deduction(5), Tracking Shuffled(5), Dyck, Word Sorting, Chinese Remainder, Schedule Meeting; 240 test instances each
claims.result_denominator: single run per cell; GPT-4+LATM on Logical Deduction 86.6 < GPT-4 CoT 88.8
claims.counterevidence: no PAL/PoT baseline; tasks have simple algorithmic solutions; contamination unchecked
claims.allowed_conclusion: For algorithmic task types, a verified Python tool built once is a large win over CoT for a weak tool user.

claims.text: LATM reduces serving cost while maintaining performance
claims.result_denominator: no measured dollars, tokens or tool-making trials cost
claims.counterevidence: tool-making retries, dispatcher and failures not priced

claims.text: A dispatcher can route instances to cached tools and detect unseen tasks
claims.counterevidence: no end-to-end stream; tool creation on cache miss not run
claims.allowed_conclusion: Routing component works on this prompt-set; closed loop untested.

claims.text: Closed-loop framework in which LLMs create their own reusable tools
claims.counterevidence: no tool update, no stream experiment
claims.allowed_conclusion: A one-shot make-then-use pipeline is demonstrated; the loop is described, not demonstrated.

assessment.strongest_supported_claim: For six algorithmic task types, a Python tool written and unit-tested by GPT-4 from 3+3 instances and reused by GPT-3.5 raises accuracy on 240 unseen instances per task far above GPT-3.5 CoT, with GPT-3.5 reaching or exceeding GPT-4 CoT on most tasks; cost saving and the closed-loop cache are not measured end to end.
unresolved: No per-instance program baseline (PAL/PoT) or verification-off arm.
Cost reduction is by formula only.
Dispatcher/growth loop not run end to end; no tool updates.

G.reason: Tool availability and serving cost are real, sourced limitations; related work covers tool-using and concurrent tool-making (Voyager, CREATOR); remaining limits are partly stated. Cost argument is not evidenced and per-instance program baselines (PAL/PoT) are cited but not treated as the nearest neighbour.

M.reason: Make-once/use-many split with test-verified tools and demonstrations is a clear mechanism with predictions that were tested (maker capacity needed, CoT reuse does not work). Verification is weak (3 validation samples) and the loop closure (cache growth) is assumed.

X.reason: The make-and-use chain is reconstructible from prompts and wrapped examples, but the retention side is thin: no update/versioning/retirement, cache-growth threshold unspecified, human-labeler fallback, no end-to-end stream implementation, dispatcher run only offline.

E.measurement.reason: Accuracy against gold answers on 240 instances per task with programmatic ground truth; one task is template-constructed by the authors and BigBench items may be contaminated.

E.causality.reason: CoT vs LATM, tool-maker and tool-user capacity ablations and a CoT-as-tool control are informative, but no per-instance program baseline for the same user, no verification-off arm, and the "tool removed" arm changes the prompting method.

E.holdout.reason: Disjoint demonstration/validation (3+3) versus 240 test instances per task; claims are limited to instances of a task type; no leakage or contamination check and no cross-task tool transfer.

E.statistics.reason: Table 2 is a single run without intervals; tool-making uses 5 trials per cell and the dispatcher 5 constructions with +/-; failures are shown in Table 3 but the tool used in Table 2 is not tied to a specific trial.

E.cost.reason: Cost is expressed as a formula with a price ratio and tool-maker retry limits; no measured tokens or dollars, tool-making failure cost, or dispatcher overhead.
